gap: No result ChatGPT got states the rated 12 V input current printed on each charger next to the 10 A (120 W) or 15 A (180 W) limit car makers put on the accessory socket, which shows the UGREEN 145W's 17.8 A label exceeds both while the Anker 75W (8 A) and Anker 535 (7.2 A) fit a 10 A socket.
standout_why: SolderMag (opened) gives per-port splits for the Anker 535, Nano 75W and Belkin but says nothing about 12 V vs 24 V input, input amps or socket fuse limits. WIRED (cited) and thisUSB/Dash & Drive could not be opened (blocked / certificate error), so their coverage is unverified; their titles and the ChatGPT answer only talk in total watts. ChargerLab and techtest.org have the raw numbers but none of the result pages convert them into a socket-limit comparison.
decides: It demotes the 145W and 167.5W 'laptop' chargers for a normal 12 V car: the UGREEN's own label asks for up to 17.8 A, above the 15 A (180 W) Polestar and 10 A (120 W) Mazda socket ratings, and techtest.org measured the Anker 167.5W's 100 W port cutting out after about 6.6 minutes. For a phone-first buyer the Anker Nano 75W (8 A at 12 V, 45 W + 30 W independent ports) is the pick that fits any socket; the Anker 535 is sold out on anker.com and drops to 9 W per port on C2 + A.
